source.title: Item Response Scaling Laws: A Measurement Theory Approach for Efficient and Generalizable Neural Scaling Estimation
source.authors: Sang T. Truong; Yuheng Tu; Rylan Schaeffer; O. Koyejo

record.file_problem: The paper text appears complete through the end of Appendix E.
record.tranche_reason: It evaluates whether downstream benchmark performance can be forecast from scale, but uses an IRT-based method and downstream metrics rather than testing the original pretraining-loss laws.
record.gate_note: The paper’s statements about earlier scaling-law results are cited background, not new results. The reported calibration simulations do not test the claim. The pretraining experiment reports decision-accuracy results by benchmark; the text gives qualitative outcomes, while the plotted values are not available in the supplied text.
record.test_reason: The study is mainly a method paper (IRSL), but it reports whether downstream benchmark rankings at 1B can be extrapolated from 4M–1B DataDecide checkpoints by traditional and IRT-based scaling fits. It explicitly states that neither approach captures reliable trends on BoolQ and HellaSwag. These are results on V6 obtained with a different method.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add that the authors say traditional pCorrect Choice scaling already performs well on high-quality benchmarks, so IRSL's gains are mainly on lower-quality ones, and that neither approach captures reliable trends on extremely noisy benchmarks (BoolQ, HellaSwag).
record.recipe_differences: The study introduces IRT/Beta-IRT estimates of latent ability and question parameters, then maps ability to downstream performance; it does not reproduce the original pretraining-loss fitting or compute-optimal allocation methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Pretraining results vary by benchmark quality and item homogeneity; Beta-IRT fails on BoolQ, HellaSwag, and WinoGrande. The paper also notes that calibration under one evaluation setup may not transfer to different conditions. The pretraining comparison includes accuracy versus probability-of-correct-choice metrics and 1PL/2PL variants.

fits_no_version.finding: With a limited query budget, IRSL estimates of −log pass@k under repeated sampling align with ground truth and have lower MAE than traditional estimates. Easy-set ability estimates also transfer to harder sets and to AIME 2025.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: IRT-based estimation can forecast test-time repeated-sampling scaling curves and transfer across test sets that share a measurement objective.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The pretraining decision-accuracy and curve-transfer results are supplied mainly as figures, without numerical values in the text. The test-time experiment is described as preliminary and uses only 12 LMs, 120 questions, and 4 benchmarks. The paper reports failures on some pretraining benchmarks and notes that calibrated item difficulties may not transfer between evaluation setups.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant pretraining rows were left out. The test-time rows record the paper’s aggregate textual findings and representative transfer examples; plotted numeric values are unavailable in the supplied text.

untested.parts: Benchmark-specific loss vs FLOP fits appear only as a figure (Fig. 13), with no exponents or assessment of the power law. Held-out pretraining loss scaling is not evaluated.
Loss extrapolation to larger runs is not evaluated. Only ranking of downstream results at 1B is extrapolated.
Other modalities, repeated data and fine-tuning are not examined. Test-time sampling does not fall under this version.

Only scales from 4M to 1B are covered, on 10 multiple-choice benchmarks. Predicting downstream performance from loss alone is not isolated. Only rank-based Decision Accuracy is reported, not absolute prediction error, for the traditional fits.
Dependence of exponents or the compute-optimal split on setup and fitting choices is not tested.

missing.what: Statement that neither traditional nor IRSL captures reliable trends on BoolQ and HellaSwag. This should be a row for the traditional method.
Ability θ scales linearly with log FLOP across all 10 benchmarks and all mixtures. This is a downstream-predictability trend.

Traditional step-1 fits of benchmark-specific loss (BPB) vs FLOP and step-2 loss-to-performance sigmoid fits (figure-only). Step 1 was fit on final checkpoints only because of the learning-rate schedule.

record.verdict_notes: The study is primarily a method paper, and most rows compare IRSL with other methods rather than measuring predictability itself. V6 verdicts rest on the paper's prose, because the Figure 3 decision-accuracy values are not in the text. The test-time experiment is described as preliminary (12 LMs, 120 questions).

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test held-out pretraining loss scaling with parameter count, tokens, or compute.
It does not test whether loss power laws fitted on small runs predict the loss of much larger runs.
It does not find or evaluate compute-optimal parameter/token allocations.
It does not compare depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
It evaluates repeated inference sampling, but does not test whether the same pretraining-loss power-law form holds in other modalities or training regimes.
It tests forecasting on the stated benchmark suites, not downstream performance generally or forecasting specifically from pretraining loss.
It discusses benchmark quality and compares fitting approaches, but does not test dependence of pretraining-loss exponents or compute-optimal splits on setup and fitting choices.

relationships.condition: High-quality benchmarks (ARC Challenge, ARC Easy, MMLU) and the easy-to-hard and cross-benchmark curve transfers, 4M–1B DataDecide models
relationships.reason: Traditional pCorrect Choice and Beta-IRT both extrapolate 1B rankings well, and hard-set curves are forecast with low MAE (r1–r3, r11–r13). All values are figure-only.
relationships.display_finding: Both pCorrect Choice and Beta-IRT extrapolated 1B model rankings well, and harder-set curves were forecast with low MAE.

relationships.reason: Predictability here depends on the fitting method: Beta-IRT outperforms the traditional and other fits (r4–r7).
relationships.display_finding: Beta-IRT outperformed traditional and alternative fits on CommonsenseQA, OpenBookQA, PIQA and SocialIQA.

relationships.reason: The authors state neither traditional nor IRSL captures reliable trends, attributed to item homogeneity (BoolQ σz=0.19) (r8, r9).
relationships.display_finding: Neither method captured reliable trends, which the authors attributed to item homogeneity, including BoolQ's σz=0.19.
